references.text: Moses instructs the people to prepare food on the day before the Sabbath, suggesting that cooking (which requires fire) should not be done on the Sabbath.
The fourth commandment to keep the Sabbath holy and rest from all work, which forms the basis for the prohibition against kindling fire.
The Sabbath command with serious consequences for violation, emphasizing the importance of refraining from work on the Sabbath.
The immediate context where Moses gathers the people and repeats the Sabbath command, which verse 3 expands upon with the specific prohibition against fire.
The account of the man who gathered wood on the Sabbath and was punished, illustrating the seriousness of Sabbath violation including activities related to fire.
Isaiah urges the people to honor the Sabbath by refraining from doing as they please and promises blessing to those who keep it holy.
Jeremiah warns against carrying burdens on the Sabbath and urges the people to keep the Sabbath holy, in line with the prohibition against work.
Jeremiah elaborates practically what 'no work' (which includes kindling fire) entails by forbidding the transport of burdens.
Along with Jeremiah 17:22, this expands the prohibition against carrying burdens and clarifies what constitutes permissible work on the Sabbath.
The general line of prohibition against 'no work' in 20:10 is the theological basis for the specific prohibition against kindling fire in 35:3.
The repetition of the Sabbath command in Deuteronomy confirms and supports the theological foundation for the prohibition against work (fire) in Exodus.
